screens.title: Libraries and Abstract Contracts
screens.subtitle: Stateless utilities and blueprint contracts for safer, reusable smart contract design

narration.text: In this lesson you will learn two powerful Solidity patterns that make smart contract code safer and more reusable: libraries and abstract contracts. Libraries let you package stateless utility functions once and reuse them across many contracts, saving bytecode and clarifying intent. Abstract contracts act as blueprints: they can require derived contracts to implement specific behaviors while still providing shared state or helper methods. Together these mechanisms let you separate utility logic from application logic, enforce standards across a suite of contracts, and reuse audited code safely. For example, you might put arithmetic checks into a SafeMath library and attach it to uint types, while defining a payment workflow in an abstract PaymentProcessor that multiple concrete processors then implement. We will show how internal and public library calls differ in storage and message context, how to deploy and link libraries during a Hardhat flow, and when to choose an interface, an abstract contract, or library. By the end you will understand trade-offs: gas, safety, and deployability, and you will be able to design a SafeMath library and a standardized vault pattern using an IVault interface plus an AbstractVault base.

keyIdea.title: What to remember
keyIdea.text: Libraries supply reusable, stateless functions and run in the caller's context; abstract contracts define required behavior while allowing shared state and implemented helpers.

Explore Key Topics
Libraries

screens.title: Why use libraries instead of inheritance?
screens.subtitle: When to choose stateless utilities over an is-a relationship

narration.text: A library in Solidity is the right choice when you need reusable, stateless functions that operate on data passed in by the caller, rather than managing their own state. Use libraries for has-a or uses-a relationships: a contract uses a library for utility behavior, while inheritance models an is-a relationship where the child contract extends the parent. A key practical reason to choose a library is reuse without duplicating bytecode: a deployed library’s code can be linked so many contracts reference the same deployed code, avoiding repetition. Libraries also make it easier to centralize audited utility logic like arithmetic checks. For example, if multiple vault contracts need safe arithmetic, defining SafeMath once and using it reduces maintenance work. A common misconception is that libraries cannot affect a contract’s state; internal library functions execute in the calling contract’s context and can operate on its storage. However, libraries themselves cannot declare storage variables or receive Ether, so they remain stateless by design. As a quick test: if you need to hold shared data or manage ownership, prefer an abstract contract or a regular contract; if you only need pure helpers, choose a library. What reusable utility would you extract from your next contract?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Libraries package stateless, reusable functions and are ideal for utility code referenced by many contracts.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Why use libraries?
Core Concept

Libraries vs Inheritance

Choose libraries for stateless helpers and inheritance for shared identity and state.

3 reasons to extract a library
  • Centralize audited logic like SafeMath to reduce duplication.
  • Save bytecode by linking to a single deployed library instance.
  • Clarify that the code is stateless and utility-only.
Common misconception
Libraries cannot declare storage, but internal library calls execute in the caller's context and can read or write the caller's storage if coded to do so.
Analogy & Example
Analogy

Think of a library as a math toolbox you keep separately and borrow functions from, versus inheritance which is like extending a toolbox into every tool you build.

Concrete Example

Multiple vault contracts can call the same SafeMath functions instead of reimplementing checks in each contract, reducing duplicated code and centralizing fixes.

Key Takeaway

Use libraries for reusable, stateless helpers; prefer abstract contracts when you need shared state or enforced behavior.

Check your understanding

If you need an owner variable shared by derived contracts, is a library sufficient? No — prefer an abstract contract.

screens.title: Library constraints and rules
screens.subtitle: What libraries can and cannot do in Solidity

narration.text: Solidity libraries have explicit constraints that shape their design. They cannot declare persistent storage variables except constants; they cannot receive Ether and they cannot inherit from other contracts. These rules exist to keep libraries stateless and safe to link into many callers. Another important rule is how functions are executed: an internal library function is inlined and runs in the calling contract’s context, operating directly on its storage if coded to do so. Public library functions are invoked with a DELEGATECALL under the hood, which means the library code executes using the calling contract’s storage, and msg. sender and msg. value are preserved from the original call. That makes public library calls powerful but also a source of risk: a buggy or malicious library can corrupt the caller’s storage because it runs using that storage and message context. A common developer error is trying to declare state in a library or expecting a library to hold Ether. When you design utilities, keep them pure or view-only and avoid state or payable functions. This reduces attack surface and keeps linking semantics predictable.

keyIdea.title: Library rules
keyIdea.text: Libraries are stateless, non-payable, non-inheriting modules whose code runs in the caller's context for both internal and DELEGATECALL-backed public functions.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Library Constraints
Definition

Library constraints

Remember these constraints when you design utilities: no state, no payable, no inheritance.

Hard rules
  • Libraries cannot have state variables (constants are allowed).
  • Libraries cannot receive Ether; avoid payable functions inside libraries.
  • Libraries cannot inherit from other contracts.
Developer pitfall
Attempting to store balances in a library or expecting it to accept Ether will fail or be insecure. Keep libraries focused on pure helpers.
Why these rules matter

Statelessness allows a single deployed library to be safely referenced by many contracts. Non-payability reduces complexity and attack vectors. Non-inheritance keeps the library API stable.

Key Takeaway

Design utilities as pure helpers. If you need storage or ownership, choose an abstract contract instead.

screens.title: Internal call vs public library call
screens.subtitle: How execution context changes and why DELEGATECALL matters

narration.text: Understanding the difference between internal and public library calls is central to safe design. An internal library function is treated by the compiler like an inline helper: its code is executed directly in the caller’s context without an external call, which is efficient and behaves like a local function. A public library function, however, results in a DELEGATECALL at runtime. DELEGATECALL executes the library code but preserves the calling contract’s storage layout and the original msg. sender and msg. value. This means that any storage writes inside the library will affect the caller's storage slots. Gas and security trade-offs follow: internal calls are cheaper and avoid external call overhead, while public calls allow code reuse without inlining but incur DELEGATECALL costs and higher risks if the library is untrusted. A common misconception is that DELEGATECALL isolates the callee; it does not. For example, if a library function assumes a particular storage slot layout and overwrites it, the calling contract could be corrupted. Always audit libraries and prefer internal, pure functions when you can. How would you decide between inlining and linking in your next contract?

keyIdea.title: Process
keyIdea.text: Internal functions are inlined; public functions use DELEGATECALL, which runs library code in the caller's storage and message context.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Internal vs Public Calls
Process Flow

Execution paths

Step 1 — Internal call

Compiler inlines the function; code runs directly in the caller with minimal overhead. This is the most gas-efficient option.

Step 2 — Public call (DELEGATECALL)

Runtime DELEGATECALL executes library code using the caller's storage, msg.sender, and msg.value. It allows a single deployed library to serve multiple callers but incurs external call cost.

Gas trade-off

Inline internal calls avoid DELEGATECALL overhead. External linking reduces bytecode but may cost more per call.

Security note

DELEGATECALL executes in the caller's storage space. A malicious library can corrupt state; only link audited libraries.

Concrete Example
If a public library function writes to slot zero, the calling contract's storage slot zero will be overwritten when called via DELEGATECALL. This can break ownership or balances if layouts differ.
Key Takeaway

Prefer internal pure functions when possible. When linking public library functions, audit storage assumptions and trust boundaries carefully.

screens.title: Math Library example
screens.subtitle: A SafeMath-style utility with overflow checks

narration.text: Let's walk through a concise Math library that implements safe arithmetic helpers. The library exposes add, sub, mul, and div as internal pure functions with require checks to prevent overflow and underflow. Each function returns the computed result and throws early when the operation would produce an invalid value. For example, add checks a plus b is at least a to catch overflow; sub checks that b is less than or equal to a; mul returns zero early for a zero operand and validates the product; div requires a nonzero divisor. Because these functions are internal and pure, they are inlined by the compiler and execute in the caller's context without DELEGATECALL overhead. When you attach such a library to the uint type using using-for, you can call a. add(b) and the first parameter becomes the instance, making the code read like a method call. A common mistake is to mark library functions payable or attempt to store intermediate state in the library — avoid that. After reviewing this code visually, try imagining where each require would trigger in a vault withdrawal or deposit flow.

keyIdea.title: Example
keyIdea.text: Math library implements safe arithmetic checks as internal pure functions to prevent overflow and underflow.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Math Library
Code Walkthrough

SafeMath-style functions

// SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
pragma solidity ^0.8.0;

library Math {
  function add(uint a, uint b) internal pure returns (uint) {
    require(a + b >= a, "Math: addition overflow");
    return a + b;
  }

  function sub(uint a, uint b) internal pure returns (uint) {
    require(b <= a, "Math: subtraction underflow");
    return a - b;
  }

  function mul(uint a, uint b) internal pure returns (uint) {
    if (a == 0) { return 0; }
    uint c = a * b;
    require(c / a == b, "Math: multiplication overflow");
    return c;
  }

  function div(uint a, uint b) internal pure returns (uint) {
    require(b > 0, "Math: division by zero");
    return a / b;
  }
}
Why pure & internal?

Pure internal functions are inlined and cause minimal gas overhead while avoiding DELEGATECALL risks.

Key Takeaway

Keep arithmetic helpers pure and internal for safety and efficiency; use require checks to guard invariants.

Concrete usage

Attach this math library to uint and call a.add(b) so arithmetic reads like a method. This pattern reduces repeated checks across multiple contracts.

Common mistake

Do not try to store balances inside the library or mark these functions payable — libraries are stateless utilities.

screens.title: using for directive and Calculator example
screens.subtitle: Attach library methods to types for cleaner code

narration.text: The using-for directive in Solidity lets you attach library functions to a type so they appear as member functions. For example, after writing using Math for uint; you can invoke add as a. add(b) and the first parameter becomes the left-hand instance, simplifying call sites and making intent clearer. This is especially helpful when you have many arithmetic operations on a particular type; the code reads like methods on the type. In the Calculator example, using Math for uint; allows result = a. add(b) and result = a. sub(b). Remember that using-for does not change semantics: it only rewrites syntax so the library function's first parameter is inferred from the instance. If you forget to include using Math for uint;, calls like a. add(b) will not compile and you must instead call Math. add(a,b). A subtle misconception is thinking using-for magically converts types; it only enables syntactic sugar. In practice, combine using-for with a carefully designed library of internal or public functions depending on your linking choice. Try both patterns in a small test to see compile-time differences. using for directive and Calculator example means using for attaches library functions to a type so the first parameter becomes the instance, improving readability and consistency.. In practical terms, attach library methods to types for cleaner code. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Pattern
keyIdea.text: using for attaches library functions to a type so the first parameter becomes the instance, improving readability and consistency.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › using for Directive
Code Walkthrough

Attach library functions to types

import "./Math.sol";

contract Calculator {
  using Math for uint; // Attach Math functions to uint

  uint public result;

  function calculateSum(uint a, uint b) public {
    result = a.add(b); // reads like a method
  }

  function calculateDifference(uint a, uint b) public {
    result = a.sub(b);
  }
}
Syntactic effect

using-for changes call syntax by binding the first parameter to the instance. It does not alter function semantics nor create new types.

Concrete tip

If you forget the using-for line, a.add(b) will fail to compile and you must call Math.add(a,b) directly. Keep your using-for directives near the consuming contract for clarity.

Key Takeaway

using-for enhances readability and encourages consistent use of shared helpers across contracts.

screens.title: Deploying and linking libraries
screens.subtitle: Deployment steps and Hardhat linking behavior

narration.text: Deploying and linking libraries is a practical step that reduces duplicated bytecode across contracts. The high-level flow is: first deploy the library as its own contract and record its address; next, link that address to dependent contract bytecode during compilation or deployment; finally, deploy the dependent contracts that reference the linked library. Development environments like Hardhat can automate this linking by resolving compile-time library references or by handling deployments in a script. Linking leads to smaller deployed bytecode for dependents because the library code is not duplicated into each contract. Keep in mind gas trade-offs at call time: internal library functions are inlined and cheap per-call but increase the caller's bytecode; linked libraries keep caller bytecode smaller but require DELEGATECALL overhead on public functions. In practice, choose inlining for hot, small helpers and linking for large, rarely changed utilities that benefit from a single audit. When writing deployment scripts, ensure you use the library address when constructing dependent artifacts so the linking is correct and deterministic. Deploying and linking libraries means deploy library once, link its address to dependent contracts, and decide between inlining vs linking based on size, change frequency, and gas profile.. In practical terms, deployment steps and hardhat linking behavior. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Deployment
keyIdea.text: Deploy library once, link its address to dependent contracts, and decide between inlining vs linking based on size, change frequency, and gas profile.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Deploy & Link
Process Flow

Deploying and linking libraries

  1. Deploy the library contract and capture its deployed address.
  2. Link the library address to dependent contract artifacts during deployment or via your build tool.
  3. Deploy dependent contracts that reference the linked library address.
Hardhat note

Hardhat can inject library addresses when you use the deployer scripts and handle linking automatically if dependencies are declared in the project configuration.

Decision guide
  • Inline small, hot helpers for lowest per-call gas.
  • Link large, shared libraries to centralize audits and reduce deploy size.
Key Takeaway

Link when you want a single audited copy of code; inline when you need minimal call cost.

screens.title: Abstract contracts explained
screens.subtitle: Blueprints with state and partial implementation

narration.text: An abstract contract in Solidity is a base contract that cannot be deployed on its own because it declares at least one function without an implementation. The abstract keyword marks intent, but contracts can become abstract by including unimplemented functions even without the keyword. Abstract contracts differ from interfaces: they may contain implemented functions, state variables, and constructors, so they can provide shared helpers while still enforcing that derived contracts implement particular behaviors. For example, a PaymentProcessor abstract contract can declare processPayment as an unimplemented function and still provide an admin state variable and a getAdmin helper. Any concrete contract inheriting from the abstract contract must implement all abstract functions to become deployable. A common error is attempting to deploy an abstract contract directly; the compiler will prevent this. Use abstract contracts when you want a shared state layout and helper logic, and use interfaces when you only need to declare external function signatures for interaction with unknown code. Abstract contracts explained means a non-deployable base contract that can include both abstract and implemented members and shared state.. In practical terms, blueprints with state and partial implementation. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Abstract contract
keyIdea.text: A non-deployable base contract that can include both abstract and implemented members and shared state.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Abstract Contracts
Definition

Abstract contracts

Use abstract contracts as blueprints that require derived contracts to implement specific behaviors but can still share state and helpers.

When to use

When you need a shared state variable or helper function across implementations and still enforce method implementations in derived classes.

Contrast with interfaces

Interfaces are purely declarative: no state, no implemented functions. Abstract contracts can mix both and therefore are more flexible for shared code models.

Key Takeaway

Choose abstract contracts to enforce behavior with shared helpers; choose interfaces when you only need a function signature to call external contracts.

screens.title: PaymentProcessor example
screens.subtitle: An abstract base with shared admin state and a required function

narration.text: The PaymentProcessor abstract contract in the source material demonstrates how to combine enforced behavior with shared helpers. It declares an immutable admin address set in a constructor and provides a getAdmin function to read it. Crucially it declares processPayment as an unimplemented virtual function that derived contracts must override. This pattern enforces a standard A P I across multiple concrete processors while centralizing the admin state and helper logic. For example, an ERC20PaymentProcessor inherits PaymentProcessor, stores an IERC20 token reference, implements processPayment by calling transferFrom on the ERC20, and then returns true. The abstract base cannot be deployed by itself; only after a concrete contract implements the missing functions does the combined contract become deployable. This architecture helps teams enforce standards: tests and code reviewers can focus on processPayment implementations knowing the admin state and getters are consistently available. A typical misconception is to duplicate admin logic in each derived contract; using the abstract base avoids that duplication and prevents logic drift. PaymentProcessor example means abstract base provides shared state and helpers; derived contracts implement the required functions to become deployable.. In practical terms, an abstract base with shared admin state and a required function. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Architecture pattern
keyIdea.text: Abstract base provides shared state and helpers; derived contracts implement the required functions to become deployable.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › PaymentProcessor
Architecture

Abstract base and concrete implementation

Abstract base

Holds shared state like admin and provides implemented helpers such as getAdmin. Declares abstract functions that derived contracts must implement.

Concrete implementation

Implements the abstract function using a storage reference such as an IERC20 token, enabling the contract to be deployed and used.

Example summary

PaymentProcessor sets admin and leaves processPayment abstract. ERC20PaymentProcessor fills in the payment logic with token transfers, adhering to the base contract's expectations.

Key Takeaway

Abstract contracts let you standardize behavior while sharing stateful helpers, reducing duplicated ownership and getter logic across implementations.

screens.title: Interfaces vs Abstract Contracts
screens.subtitle: When to use a pure interface or an abstract base

narration.text: Interfaces and abstract contracts are both ways to specify expected behavior, but they serve different purposes. Interfaces are purely declarative: they declare function signatures with no implementations, no state variables, and no constructors. Use interfaces when you need to interact with external contracts whose implementation you don't control or when you want a compact A P I descriptor like IERC20. Abstract contracts can include both unimplemented functions and implemented helpers, state variables, and constructors. Use abstract contracts when you want a shared state layout or helper functions that derived contracts inherit. A practical contrast: if you only need a stable function set to call an external token, define an interface; if you need to enforce ownership and provide common getter functions, use an abstract contract. Errors occur when developers try to store state inside interfaces or attempt to deploy an abstract contract with unimplemented functions. Decide based on whether you require shared logic and state (choose abstract) or only a signature for external interaction (choose interface). Which option better matches your need to share state? Interfaces vs Abstract Contracts means interfaces declare signatures only; abstract contracts can include state and implemented functions in addition to abstract methods.. In practical terms, when to use a pure interface or an abstract base. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Comparison
keyIdea.text: Interfaces declare signatures only; abstract contracts can include state and implemented functions in addition to abstract methods.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Interface vs Abstract
Interface

Purely declarative

Defines external function signatures only. No state, no implementation. Use to talk to unknown contracts like ERC20 tokens.

Example
interface IERC20 { function transfer(address recipient, uint256 amount) external returns (bool); }
Abstract Contract

Blueprint with state

Can include implemented functions, state variables, and constructors. Enforces that derived contracts implement abstract members before deploy.

Key Takeaway

Use interfaces for external interaction and abstract contracts for shared implementation plus enforced behavior.

screens.title: Designing a Safe Vault using SafeMath and IVault
screens.subtitle: Scaffold SafeMath, IVault, AbstractVault, and SimpleEtherVault

narration.text: This hands-on activity ties the chapter together: build a SafeMath library, define an IVault interface, create an AbstractVault base, and implement a SimpleEtherVault concrete contract. Start with SafeMath: implement add, sub, mul, div with require checks to avoid overflow and division by zero. Next define IVault as a minimal external A P I with deposit, withdraw, balanceOf, and totalVaultBalance. The AbstractVault implements IVault partially: it uses SafeMath for uint, provides a balances mapping, sets an owner in the constructor, and implements balanceOf and totalVaultBalance as the contract’s Ether balance. Leave deposit and withdraw declared virtual so derived contracts must implement them. Finally, implement SimpleEtherVault to accept Ether on deposit, update balances with SafeMath, and perform withdrawals with onlyOwner protection. A common pitfall is mixing owner access semantics: the example uses onlyOwner on withdraw to illustrate an ownership restriction; in your design consider who should be allowed to withdraw. These steps will help you practice attaching a library, enforcing an interface, and designing a secure concrete implementation. Designing a Safe Vault using SafeMath and IVault means implement safemath, an ivault interface, an abstractvault base with balances and owner, and a simpleethervault that uses safemath for arithmetic.. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Key Concepts — What to Remember
screens.subtitle: Three essential ideas from this chapter

narration.text: Let's summarize the three essential ideas. First: Libraries are stateless utilities designed for reuse; prefer pure or internal functions and avoid storing state or accepting Ether. Second: using-for lets you attach library functions to a type so calls read like member methods; this improves readability and helps standardize behavior. Third: Abstract contracts act as blueprints with shared state and helper implementations; interfaces are purely declarative and should be used when only function signatures are required. Together these concepts let you design secure and maintainable contracts by centralizing audited logic, enforcing common APIs, and selecting the right abstraction for shared state. As you practice the hands-on vault exercise, ask whether a piece of logic should live in a library, an abstract contract, or a concrete contract, and use those answers to guide safe architecture decisions.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Key Concepts
Library

Stateless utilities, no persistent storage, and designed for reuse and linking.

using for

Attaches library functions to a type so they can be called with instance.method() syntax.

Abstract Contract

Blueprints with optional implemented helpers and state; derived contracts must implement abstract functions.

Summary takeaway

Choose the right abstraction: library for stateless helpers, interface for external signatures, and abstract contract for shared state and partial implementations.

screens.title: Key Concepts — Quick Reference
screens.subtitle: Three short reminders before you code

narration.text: Before you begin coding, keep three quick reminders in mind. First: libraries are stateless — do not place storage or payable behavior there. Second: public library calls involve DELEGATECALL which runs in the caller's storage context, so link only trusted libraries. Third: abstract contracts provide shared state and implemented helpers while enforcing abstract methods; use interfaces when you only need an external function signature. These reminders will help you avoid the most common mistakes and choose the right structure for maintainable, auditable Solidity code. content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Quick Reference
No state in libs

Keep libraries pure or view-only; store state in contracts.

DELEGATECALL caution

Public library calls run in the caller's storage; audit linked libraries.

Abstract vs Interface

Choose abstract for shared state; choose interface for external signatures only.

Final thought

Design with reuse and trust boundaries in mind: centralize audited helpers in libraries and require implementations through abstract contracts when necessary.
